issues.legal_issue: The revisional jurisdiction of a rent-control court permits review of the legality and propriety of an appellate order but does not permit the revisional court to act as a second appellate court on factual findings.
material_facts: The appellate authority reversed the eviction order after considering the evidence and finding that exclusive possession had not been established.
The High Court, exercising rent-control revisional jurisdiction, reassessed the evidence and reversed the appellate authority’s finding.
The Supreme Court found that the appellate authority’s conclusion was supported by the evidence and was not perverse.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s revisional power was wider than the jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but it could not substitute its own factual assessment unless the appellate authority’s appreciation of evidence was perverse or its conclusion was one no reasonable person could reach on the materials.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 permits the High Court to examine the legality and propriety of an order, including the correctness of factual findings in an appropriate case, but does not confer appellate jurisdiction. Smt. Rajbir Kaur v. M/s. S. Chokesiri & Co. establishes that a revisional court should not supplant a finding supported by the evidence; Nanak Chand v. Inderjit recognises the breadth of the statutory power; and Ram Das v. Ishwar Chander describes it as wider than Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure while remaining subject to the limits inherent in revision.

rule.if: rent_control_revision and appellate_finding_supported_by_evidence and not appellate_finding_perverse

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding is a revision of an appellate order in a rent-control matter.
predicates.appellate_finding_supported_by_evidence: The appellate authority’s factual finding is supported by evidence in the record.
predicates.appellate_finding_perverse: The appellate authority’s appreciation of the evidence is perverse or its conclusion is one no reasonable person could reach on the record.

issues.definition: When a rent-control revision challenges a factual finding supported by the record and that finding is not perverse, the revisional court must not replace it with its own factual assessment.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant is not liable to eviction for subletting merely because another person conducts business in the premises; subletting requires proof that the tenant parted with legal possession, including the alleged subtenant’s exclusive possession.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground that other persons had been given the premises and were conducting business there.
The tenant maintained that he continued his own business and also acted as a commission agent for a business associated with one of the other occupants.
The evidence included a commissioner’s report that recorded a sale under another business name, but also recorded a bill-book identifying the tenant as sole selling agent.
The commissioner testified that the landlord’s representative supplied the money for the purchase and received the purchased cloth from the commissioner.
The evidence did not establish that the other persons had exclusive possession or that the tenant had parted with possession.
issues.conclusion: The landlord failed to prove subletting. The High Court’s finding of subletting was unsustainable, the eviction order on that ground was set aside, and the appellate authority’s order dismissing the eviction application was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 requires proof of subletting. The burden of establishing subletting rests on the landlord. Under Jagdish Prasad v. Angoori Devi, another person’s presence in business premises alone does not establish subletting where the tenant retains control and conducts business there. M/s. Shalimar Tar Products Ltd. v. H.C. Sharma explains that parting with legal possession entails a right to include and exclude others. Smt. Rajbir Kaur v. M/s. S. Chokesiri & Co. recognises that exclusive possession may permit an inference of consideration in a clandestine transaction, but the burden remains on the landlord. Here, exclusive possession was not established, and the commissioner’s evidence was tainted by the landlord’s involvement.

predicates.rent_eviction_case_based_on_alleged_subl: The proceeding seeks eviction from rented premises on the ground that the tenant sublet them.
predicates.alleged_subtenant_exclusive_possession_n: The evidence does not establish that the alleged subtenant had exclusive possession of the premises.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding based on alleged subletting, the ground is not established when the evidence fails to prove the alleged subtenant’s exclusive possession.
